front: What gates must every item of evidence pass on an Evidence essay?
back: Relevance; 403/§ 352; character, policy and privilege rules; witness issues; authentication and best/secondary evidence; hearsay for each layer; confrontation if criminal; limiting instruction.

front: Which law governs a California Evidence essay?
back: Whatever the call names: the FRE or the California Evidence Code (it switches between exams). The MBE uses only the FRE as currently in effect.
Any tendency to make a fact of consequence more or less probable. CEC § 210 adds that the fact must be disputed and includes credibility of witnesses and hearsay declarants.
Court may exclude relevant evidence if probative value is substantially outweighed by unfair prejudice, confusion, misleading the jury, undue delay/consumption of time, or cumulative evidence.

front: What does California's Truth-in-Evidence provision do?
back: In criminal proceedings relevant evidence shall not be excluded, except under hearsay and privilege rules, §§ 352, 782, 1103, and statutes passed after 1982 by two-thirds vote (Cal. Const. art. I, § 28(f)(2)).
Yes. The Legislature re-enacted § 1101 by a two-thirds vote in 1986 (People v. Ewoldt (1994) 7 Cal.4th 380).

front: Does Prop 8 apply in civil cases?
back: No — only criminal proceedings (including pretrial and post-conviction hearings and juvenile criminal cases).

front: Who decides whether a hearsay exception's foundation is met, and by what standard?
back: The judge, by a preponderance, not bound by evidence rules except privilege (FRE 104(a); Bourjaily; CEC § 405).
When relevance depends on a fact (authenticity, personal knowledge), the judge admits it if there is evidence sufficient to support a finding; the jury decides (FRE 104(b); CEC § 403).

front: When must the court give a limiting instruction?
back: On timely request, when evidence is admissible for one purpose or party but not another (FRE 105; CEC § 355).

front: How is error in admitting evidence preserved?
back: Timely objection or motion to strike stating the specific ground (unless apparent); for exclusion, an offer of proof (FRE 103; CEC §§ 353–354).

front: Must a defendant testify to appeal a ruling that his conviction can impeach him?
back: Yes — Luce v. United States (1984). And introducing it himself on direct waives appeal (Ohler).
Lay witness must have perceived the matter; evidence sufficient to support a finding, which can be the witness's own testimony (FRE 602; CEC § 702).

front: California's two grounds for disqualifying a witness?
back: Incapable of expressing himself so as to be understood, or incapable of understanding the duty to tell the truth (CEC § 701).

front: FRE 606(b): what may jurors testify about to impeach a verdict?
back: Extraneous prejudicial information, outside influence, or a mistake on the verdict form — plus the Peña-Rodriguez racial-bias exception. Not deliberations or mental processes.

front: How does CEC § 1150 differ from FRE 606(b)?
back: § 1150 admits evidence of statements, conduct, conditions or events (overt acts) likely to have improperly influenced the verdict, but not their effect on mental processes.

front: FRE 612 vs. CEC § 771 on writings used to refresh before testifying?
back: FRE: production only if justice requires. CEC: mandatory on request whether used before or while testifying; otherwise testimony stricken.

front: Is the item used to refresh recollection evidence?
back: No. The witness testifies from revived memory. Only the adverse party may introduce relevant portions.
Rationally based on perception; helpful; not based on scientific, technical or specialized knowledge.

front: Effect of judicial notice in civil vs. criminal cases (FRE 201(f))?
back: Civil: jury must accept as conclusive. Criminal: jury may, but need not, accept it.

front: Effect of a civil presumption under FRE 301?
back: Shifts only the burden of producing evidence; burden of persuasion stays put (bursting bubble).

front: Which California presumptions shift the burden of proof?
back: Those implementing public policy (§§ 605–606), e.g., § 662 title presumption (clear and convincing to rebut). Others affect only the burden of production (§ 604).

front: Why is a mandatory presumption of intent unconstitutional in a criminal case?
back: It relieves the prosecution of proving an element beyond a reasonable doubt (Sandstrom v. Montana).
Subject matter of direct plus credibility; court may allow more as if on direct (FRE 611(b); CEC § 773).

front: When are leading questions allowed on direct?
back: When necessary to develop testimony (preliminary matters, children, forgetful witness) and when calling a hostile witness, adverse party, or witness identified with an adverse party.

front: Who may not be excluded under FRE 615?
back: A natural-person party; an entity's designated representative; a person essential to the case; a person authorized by statute.

front: What did the 2023 amendment add to FRE 615?
back: Court may order excluded witnesses not to receive or access trial testimony.

front: May a party impeach its own witness?
back: Yes (FRE 607; CEC § 785).
Extrinsic evidence of a prior inconsistent statement only after the witness has had a chance to explain or deny (unless court orders otherwise); not for an opposing party's statement.

front: CEC § 770 foundation for extrinsic proof of an inconsistent statement?
back: Witness was given an opportunity to explain or deny, OR has not been excused from giving further testimony.
Never. Extrinsic evidence is allowed (usually after a foundation question) (United States v. Abel).

front: FRE 609(a)(1) balancing for a criminal defendant vs. other witnesses?
back: Defendant: probative value must outweigh prejudicial effect to the defendant. Other witnesses: Rule 403.
Any crime whose elements required a dishonest act or false statement must be admitted — felony or misdemeanor, no balancing.
If >10 years since conviction or release (later), admissible only if probative value substantially outweighs prejudice, with written notice.
Felony involving moral turpitude (least adjudicated elements), subject to § 352 (People v. Castro; art. I, § 28(f)(4)).

front: Can misdemeanor conduct impeach in a California criminal case?
back: Yes, if it involves moral turpitude, subject to § 352 (People v. Wheeler) — but the misdemeanor conviction record itself was hearsay.

front: Felony impeachment in California civil cases?
back: § 788 permits felony convictions, subject to § 352; criminal moral-turpitude cases are guidelines (Robbins v. Wong). Misdemeanors not admissible.
Inquiry on cross if probative of truthfulness; no extrinsic evidence; take the answer.
Civil: inadmissible even on cross (§ 787). Criminal: moral-turpitude conduct admissible under Prop 8, subject to § 352.

front: When may a party offer evidence of a witness's truthful character?
back: Only after the witness's character for truthfulness has been attacked (FRE 608(a); CEC § 790).
Any evidence admissible if the declarant had testified; inconsistent statements need no chance to explain (FRE 806; CEC § 1202).
A prior consistent statement offered to rebut recent fabrication must have been made before the motive to fabricate arose.
Only on non-collateral matters (relevant to a substantive issue or independently admissible to impeach).

front: Where do the FRE not apply?
back: Preliminary fact-finding under 104(a), grand jury, sentencing, probation revocation, extradition, preliminary examinations, warrants, bail — but privileges always apply.
Character or a trait is not admissible to prove conduct in conformity on a particular occasion (FRE 404(a)(1); CEC § 1101(a)).
When it is an element: defamation (truth), negligent entrustment/hiring, custody, entrapment. Any method, including specific acts.
Defendant may offer a pertinent trait by reputation or opinion; prosecution may then rebut (FRE 404(a)(2)(A); CEC § 1102).

front: Victim's character — FRE vs. CEC method?
back: FRE: reputation or opinion only. CEC § 1103(a): opinion, reputation, or specific instances.

front: Consequence of offering the victim's violent character?
back: FRE: prosecution may rebut and show defendant's same trait. CEC § 1103(b): prosecution may prove defendant's violence by any method.
Prosecution may show victim's peacefulness to rebut any evidence the victim was the first aggressor.

front: How may a character witness be cross-examined?
back: 'Have you heard' / 'did you know' about relevant specific acts, with a good-faith basis; no extrinsic proof (Michelson).
Habit = specific, regular, semi-automatic response to a recurring situation; admissible (FRE 406; § 1105). Character = general disposition; barred.
Motive, intent, absence of mistake/lack of accident, identity, common plan — plus opportunity, preparation, knowledge.
Admit if a jury could reasonably find by a preponderance that the act occurred (104(b)); acquittal is no bar.
Least similarity for intent; more for common design or plan; most (distinctive) for identity.
In criminal cases, prosecution must give reasonable written notice before trial, stating the permitted purpose and the reasoning.
In sexual-assault or child-molestation cases, other such acts are admissible for propensity, subject to 403/§ 352. CEC: criminal only.
In criminal DV cases, other DV acts admissible for propensity subject to § 352; acts > 10 years old excluded unless interest of justice. No FRE counterpart.
Source of semen/injury/physical evidence; sexual behavior with the defendant on consent; constitutionally required evidence.
Admissible only if probative value substantially outweighs harm to victim and unfair prejudice; reputation only if victim placed it in controversy.
To attack the complainant's credibility with sexual conduct: written motion, offer of proof, sworn affidavit, hearing outside the jury, § 352.
Defendant's creative expression is presumed to have minimal literal-truth value absent specified links; weigh racial-bias and propensity risks; hearing outside jury.
Evidence sufficient to support a finding that the item is what the proponent claims (FRE 901(a); CEC §§ 1400–1401).

front: Lay handwriting vs. voice identification familiarity?
back: Handwriting familiarity must not be acquired for litigation; voice familiarity may be acquired at any time.

front: Ancient documents — FRE vs. CEC age?
back: FRE 901(b)(8): 20 years. California presumption: 30 years.
Sealed public documents; certified copies of public records; newspapers/periodicals; trade inscriptions; notarized documents (also commercial paper, certified business and electronic records).

front: Is a red-light camera photo hearsay in California?
back: No — machine-generated; §§ 1552–1553 presume accuracy (People v. Goldsmith (2014)).
Allowed if utility is not substantially outweighed by prejudice, confusion or delay; not evidence; not in jury room without consent or good cause.
Proponent must show the court it is more likely than not that the expert is helpful, uses sufficient facts, reliable methods, and reliable application.

front: Can experts rely on inadmissible facts?
back: Yes, if experts in the field reasonably rely on them; proponent may disclose them only if probative value in evaluating the opinion substantially outweighs prejudice (FRE 703).
An expert may not relate case-specific hearsay as true unless independently proven or excepted; if testimonial, Crawford applies.
In a criminal case an expert may not opine whether the defendant had the mental state constituting an element or defense.
Pen. Code § 29 (guilt phase: no expert testimony on whether defendant had required mental state). § 805 otherwise allows ultimate-issue opinions.
Testability; peer review/publication; error rate; standards; general acceptance.
New scientific technique: general acceptance in the relevant scientific community; qualified witness; correct procedures used. Survived Daubert (Leahy).
Trial court excludes expert opinion based on matter not reasonably relied on, reasons unsupported by the material, or speculation.

front: Source of privilege law in federal court?
back: Federal common law under FRE 501; state law for claims where state law supplies the rule of decision (diversity).

front: Source of privilege law in California?
back: Statutes only (§ 911); courts cannot create privileges.
Confidential communication between client and lawyer (or representatives) for legal advice; client holds; facts not privileged.
Upjohn: employee communications at superiors' direction for legal advice. Chadbourne: employer's dominant purpose; employee as corporate representative vs. independent witness.
No privilege if the client sought or used the lawyer's services to commit or plan a crime or fraud (future or ongoing).
No lawyer-client privilege where the lawyer reasonably believes disclosure is necessary to prevent a criminal act likely to cause death or substantial bodily harm.
Attorney's impressions, conclusions, opinions, theories: absolutely protected; other work product only if denial unfairly prejudices or causes injustice; attorney holds (CCP § 2018.030).
No waiver if inadvertent, holder took reasonable steps to prevent, and promptly took reasonable steps to rectify.
Criminal cases; witness-spouse holds and may refuse or choose to testify; requires valid marriage at time of testimony.
Privilege not to testify against spouse and not to be called by adverse party, in any proceeding (§§ 970–971); witness-spouse holds.
Confidential communications during marriage; both spouses hold; survives divorce and death; civil and criminal.
No federal privilege. California § 994 — but not in criminal proceedings (§ 998) and not where patient tenders condition (§ 996).
Federal (Jaffee): includes clinical social workers; no balancing. California § 1014 applies in criminal cases too; dangerous-patient exception § 1024.

front: FRE 411 permitted purposes for insurance evidence?
back: Bias or prejudice of a witness; agency, ownership, or control.

front: FRE 407 vs. CEC § 1151 in strict products liability?
back: FRE 407 excludes repairs to prove product defect. California § 1151 does not apply to strict liability (Ault) — admissible.
Impeachment; and, if disputed, ownership, control, or feasibility of precautions.
A disputed claim (validity or amount); offers and statements in negotiation excluded to prove validity/amount or to impeach by inconsistency.

front: FRE 409 vs. FRE 408 on accompanying statements?
back: 409: offer to pay medical expenses excluded but accompanying statements admissible. 408: negotiation statements excluded too.
Expressions of sympathy about an accident victim's pain, suffering or death are inadmissible to prove liability in a civil action; statements of fault are not excluded by § 1160.
Withdrawn guilty pleas, nolo pleas, statements in Rule 11 proceedings on them, and plea discussions with a prosecuting attorney — against the defendant.

front: When does the best evidence rule apply?
back: Only when proving the content of a writing, recording or photograph — legally operative documents or knowledge derived from the writing.

front: When is a duplicate not admissible under FRE 1003?
back: When a genuine question is raised about the original's authenticity, or admitting the duplicate would be unfair.
Originals lost/destroyed without bad faith; not obtainable by process; opponent controls and fails to produce after notice; collateral matter.
Content may be proved by otherwise admissible secondary evidence unless a genuine dispute on material terms and justice requires exclusion, or admission would be unfair.

front: CEC § 1523 oral testimony of a writing's content?
back: Inadmissible unless original lost/destroyed without proponent's fraud, not reasonably procurable, collateral, or numerous accounts (general result).
Summaries of voluminous admissible evidence are admissible as evidence whether or not the underlying evidence was admitted; underlying material must be available.
Completeness covers written and oral statements; the completing part comes in at that time, over a hearsay objection.
A statement (assertion) made other than while testifying at the current trial or hearing, offered to prove the truth of the matter asserted (FRE 801(c); CEC § 1200).
No — it is not a 'statement' (FRE 801(a); CEC § 225).
Verbal acts; effect on listener/notice; circumstantial state of mind; impeachment (and showing a statement was false).
Any prior inconsistent statement of a testifying witness subject to cross is not hearsay — substantive, subject to 403 and 613(b). Old rule required oath at a proceeding.
Prior inconsistent statement of a testifying witness admissible for its truth if § 770 is satisfied. Feigned memory loss counts as inconsistency (People v. Green).
Rebut charge of recent fabrication/improper motive (pre-motive statement), or rehabilitate when credibility attacked on another ground.
Made when the event was fresh in memory, and the witness testifies he made it and it truly reflected his opinion then.

front: Party admission — personal knowledge or against interest needed?
back: Neither. Only that it was made by the party and is offered against that party.

front: Label for party admissions under FRE vs. CEC?
back: FRE: not hearsay (exclusion). CEC: hearsay within the § 1220 exception.
Party heard and understood, could respond, and a reasonable person would have denied; not after Miranda warnings (Doyle).
FRE 801(d)(2)(D): agent/employee on matter within scope, during relationship. CEC: only if authorized (§ 1222) or derivative liability (§ 1224).
During and in furtherance of the conspiracy; conspiracy and membership shown by preponderance; statement considered but not alone (Bourjaily).
Each layer must satisfy an exclusion or exception (FRE 805; CEC § 1201).

front: Does California have a present sense impression exception?
back: No general one. § 1241 covers only statements explaining the declarant's own conduct while engaged in it.
Startling event; statement relating to (CEC: narrating, describing, explaining) it; made under the stress of excitement.

front: Then-existing state of mind — what is excluded?
back: Statements of memory or belief to prove the fact remembered (Shepard), except about the declarant's will.
Statement of present intent is admissible to show the declarant probably carried it out.
Statement of the declarant's prior mental or physical state, if declarant unavailable and that state is in issue.
Statements for and reasonably pertinent to diagnosis or treatment: history, symptoms, inception, general cause — not fault; to anyone.
Medical-diagnosis statements only by a minor victim who made them when under 12, describing child abuse or neglect.
Once knew; now cannot recall fully; made/adopted when fresh; accurate. Read into evidence; exhibit only if offered by adverse party (FRE 803(5); CEC § 1237).
Made at or near the time by someone with knowledge; regular course; regular practice; custodian or certification; opponent fails to show untrustworthiness.
§ 1271 covers acts, conditions, events (opinions/diagnoses excluded — Reyes) and the proponent must show trustworthiness.
A report prepared in anticipation of litigation is not a trustworthy business record.
Matters observed by law-enforcement personnel are excluded in criminal cases; investigative findings usable only in civil cases or against the government.
FRE 803(18): substantive if established as reliable and used with an expert; read, not received. CEC: no exception; § 721(b) cross-examination only.
Privilege; refusal despite order; lack of memory; death or illness; absence despite process/reasonable means.
Unavailable; testimony at trial, hearing or deposition; party (or civil predecessor in interest) had opportunity and similar motive to develop it.
In civil actions, former testimony is admissible against a non-party to the earlier proceeding if a party there had similar interest and motive to cross.

front: Statement against interest — what does California add?
back: Social interest: risk of hatred, ridicule or social disgrace (§ 1230).
Only the self-inculpatory portions of a statement against interest are admissible; collateral and blame-shifting parts are excluded.
In criminal cases, corroborating circumstances clearly indicating trustworthiness, judged by the totality of circumstances and evidence supporting or undermining it.
FRE: homicide prosecutions or civil cases; declarant unavailable (need not die). CEC § 1242: any case; declarant must have died.
Party who wrongfully caused unavailability intending to prevent testimony forfeits hearsay and confrontation objections.
FRE 807: trustworthiness (totality + corroboration), more probative than other reasonably available evidence, notice. California has none.
Unavailable declarant; narrates infliction or threat of injury on declarant; at or near the time; within 5 years; trustworthy; written, recorded, or to medical or police personnel.
Testimonial hearsay of a non-testifying declarant is barred unless the declarant is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity to cross-examine.
Testimonial if the primary purpose is to establish past events for prosecution; nontestimonial if to meet an ongoing emergency (Davis; Bryant; Clark).
Forensic certificates are testimonial; the analyst must testify; a surrogate analyst is not enough.
In a joint trial, a nontestifying codefendant's confession that facially incriminates the defendant is inadmissible even with an instruction.
Face-to-face confrontation may yield only on a case-specific finding that a child witness would be traumatized by the defendant's presence.
Mechanical application of hearsay and voucher rules to exclude reliable, critical defense evidence violates due process.
